\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty.
A full bootstrap procedure (re-estimating both the confusion matrix and the downstream estimator per replicate, $B{=}100$) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even the plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% coverage at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$, confirming the method's reliability across the practical range (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.86 at the subgroup level (Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix).
On real LLM confusion matrices (16 combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}), AUC decreases to 0.63, primarily from subgroups with $\tau_s \approx 0$ where both naive and corrected bias are near zero, making the ground-truth harm label indeterminate; on subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$, AUC reaches 1.0.
For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces ranking by $1/\pi_s$ alone, which can anti-predict harm; reliability is strongest for $K{\geq}4$.
A computable meta-criterion recovers reliability: when $\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) > 1$, the diagnostic achieves AUC $\geq 0.75$ across all 16 combinations; when $\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) \leq 1$, AUC drops to 0.0--0.67 (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).

A recommended practitioner workflow and budget crossover curves appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:screening}.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$, EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing a practical scalability boundary (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
The bias identity further validates across eight LLMs spanning 11 model--dataset combinations ($R^2 = 0.975$; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).

\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our effect-modifier setting differs because the proxy ($\hat{Z}$) replaces a moderator rather than a confounder, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
Our problem is structurally distinct: the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting correction through confusion matrices.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.

Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.
Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.
The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
\citet{miao2018identifying} develop proximal causal inference for unmeasured confounders using proxy variables; our effect-modifier setting differs because the proxy ($\hat{Z}$) replaces a moderator rather than a confounder, admitting confusion-matrix correction without the identification constraints of the proximal framework.
Our problem is structurally distinct: the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting correction through confusion matrices.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We derived a bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces subgroup-level bias proportional to $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$, worsening CATE estimates in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations.
EC-HTE provides subgroup-stratified correction via hierarchical Bayes; the companion diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$) flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup misclassification rates.
EC-HTE's advantage requires sufficient $\Delta\pi$ and expert budget.
More broadly, the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates serves as an effect modifier---survey coding, medical diagnosis from proxy tests, and satellite imagery classification all face analogous misclassification heterogeneity when constructing effect modifiers for HTE analysis.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We derived a bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces subgroup-level bias proportional to $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$, worsening CATE estimates in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations.
EC-HTE provides subgroup-stratified correction via hierarchical Bayes; the companion diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$) flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup misclassification rates.
EC-HTE's advantage requires sufficient $\Delta\pi$ and expert budget.
More broadly, the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates serves as an effect modifier---survey coding, medical diagnosis, and satellite imagery classification all share this structure.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	
7	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
8	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
9	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
10	Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, and outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}).
11	
12	\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
13	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
14	
15	We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
16	Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
17	Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
18	
19	\begin{figure*}[t]
20	\centering
21	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
22	\caption{Bias amplification under global correction ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: correction always helps. (b) High-error subgroup: correction \emph{increases} bias when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (hatched), reaching 2.86$\times$.}
23	\label{fig:heatmap}
24	\end{figure*}
25	
26	\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
27	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
28	
29	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
30	Notably, in the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058)---a direct manifestation of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}: pooled correction overshoots in low-error subgroups.
31	F-L scalar correction ($\hat{\tau}/(1{-}2\bar{\pi})$) increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 with coverage 0.68---worse than naive---because a single scalar cannot correct heterogeneous attenuation; F-L per-subgroup inflates bias to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
32	HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
33	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
34	In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($K{=}4$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$), EC-HTE and Global achieve comparable $|\text{bias}|$ ($p{=}0.395$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}), but EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124), driven by moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and unbalanced subgroups receiving ${\sim}30$ expert labels each.
35	When $\Delta\pi$ or per-subgroup budget is marginal, global correction is competitive on aggregate RMSE.
36	
37	\paragraph{CausalForest.}
38	With CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$), improving coverage from 0.58 to 0.90; global correction amplifies naive bias up to 5.9$\times$ because the forest magnifies label errors (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
39	The residual coverage gap (90\% vs.\ oracle 94--96\%) reflects asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation rather than CM estimation error; a full bootstrap SE can improve coverage calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
40	
41	\begin{table}[t]
42	\centering
43	\caption{Main results (extreme heterogeneity). Metrics averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, 100 MC runs. Bold: lowest $|\text{bias}|$. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global. Moderate heterogeneity and TweetEval results---where methods converge and EC-HTE RMSE exceeds Global---in Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}; MC SEs in Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}.}
44	\label{tab:main_results}
45	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
46	\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}
47	\toprule
48	Configuration & Method & $|\text{Bias}|$ & RMSE & 95\% CI Cov. \\
49	\midrule
50	\multirow{6}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}2$, $n{=}250$}}
51	 & Naive & 0.058 & 0.090 & 0.82 \\
52	 & Global & 0.059 & 0.099 & 0.87 \\
53	 & F-L Scalar & 0.122 & 0.159 & 0.68 \\
54	 & F-L Per-sub. & 0.168 & 0.220 & 0.65 \\
55	 & Strat.\ MLE & 0.012 & 0.094 & 0.95 \\

1	% Requires preamble: \usepackage{amsthm,amsmath,amssymb}
2	% and: \newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
3	%      \newtheorem{corollary}[theorem]{Corollary}
4	%      \newtheorem{proposition}[theorem]{Proposition}
5	
6	\section{Bias Decomposition: When Debiasing Hurts}
7	\label{sec:theory}
8	
9	We formalize the bias that global misclassification correction introduces when subgroup error rates are heterogeneous.
10	Consider estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) $\tau(z) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid Z = z]$, where $Z \in \{0, 1\}$ is a binary effect modifier observed only through a noisy annotation $\hat{Z}$.
11	The population consists of $K$ subgroups $S \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ with weights $w_s = P(S{=}s)$, each characterized by a $2 \times 2$ confusion matrix $C_s$ with symmetric error rate $\pi_s = P(\hat{Z} \neq Z \mid S{=}s)$.
12	Standard practice estimates a single confusion matrix $\bar{C} = \sum_s w_s C_s$ from expert annotations and applies its inverse uniformly to all observations, with pooled error rate $\bar{\pi} = \sum_s w_s \pi_s$.
13	We show that when error rates vary across subgroups, this global procedure introduces a bias with an exact product form.
14	
15	We state five assumptions maintained throughout.
16	%
17	\begin{itemize}
18	\item[\textbf{(A1)}] \textit{Conditional independence:} misclassification depends only on the true label $Z$ and subgroup $S$, not on potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1)$.
19	\item[\textbf{(A2)}] \textit{Symmetric misclassification:} $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}0, S{=}s) = P(\hat{Z}{=}0 \mid Z{=}1, S{=}s) = \pi_s$ for all $s$ (diagnostic only; see Remark~2).
20	\item[\textbf{(A3)}] \textit{Balanced effect modifier:} $P(Z{=}0) = P(Z{=}1) = 0.5$. This simplifies the exposition; we discuss relaxation below.
21	\item[\textbf{(A4)}] \textit{Non-degeneracy:} $\pi_s \neq 0.5$ for all $s$, ensuring each $C_s$ is invertible.
22	\item[\textbf{(A5)}] \textit{Homogeneous treatment effects across subgroups:} $\tau(z, s) = \tau(z)$ for all $s$, so $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is a scalar.
23	\end{itemize}
24	
25	Under (A2)--(A3), the Bayesian mixing matrix $M_s$ (entries $M_s[\hat{z}, z] = P(Z{=}z \mid \hat{Z}{=}\hat{z}, S{=}s)$) coincides with $C_s$.
26	The global mixing matrix is $M_{\text{global}} = \sum_s w_s M_s$.
27	
28	\begin{theorem}[Bias Decomposition Identity]
29	\label{thm:bias_identity}
30	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, the bias of global correction in subgroup $s$ at effect-modifier level $z$ is
31	\begin{align}
32	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}0, s) &= +\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z0} \\
33	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}1, s) &= -\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z1}
34	\end{align}
35	where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$ is the subgroup deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is the CATE heterogeneity.
36	\end{theorem}
37	
38	Equations~\eqref{eq:bias_z0}--\eqref{eq:bias_z1} constitute an exact finite-population identity, not an asymptotic approximation or bound.
39	The bias factors into three interpretable components: $\delta_s$ captures how much subgroup $s$ deviates from the average misclassification rate, $\Delta\tau$ captures treatment effect heterogeneity across levels of $Z$, and $1/(1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ is an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
40	Bias vanishes when either source of variation is absent ($\delta_s = 0$ or $\Delta\tau = 0$), and arises only through their interaction.
41	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} implies that global correction trades one source of confounding for another: it removes attenuation from label noise but introduces a new bias from error-rate heterogeneity.
42	
43	\paragraph{Proof sketch.}
44	Global correction applies $M_{\text{global}}^{-1}$ to the subgroup-specific observed CATE $\tau_{\text{obs}}(\cdot, s) = M_s \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$, yielding bias $(M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I) \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$.
45	Direct computation shows $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I = \frac{\delta_s}{1-2\bar{\pi}} \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$.
46	Applying this matrix to $[\tau(0),\, \tau(1)]^\top$ produces the product form.
47	The full derivation appears in Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}.
48	For comparison with classical scalar attenuation~\citep{frazis2003estimating}, see Section~\ref{sec:related}.
49	
50	\paragraph{Relationship to classical scalar attenuation.}
51	Classical scalar attenuation~\citep{frazis2003estimating} gives $\beta^* = \beta(1 - 2\pi)$; dividing by $(1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ removes this bias under homogeneous errors, but Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity: \emph{correction-induced} bias from applying $M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1}$ to heterogeneous $M_s$.
52	F-L scalar correction (dividing $\hat{\tau}(z)$ by $1 - 2\bar{\pi}$) over-corrects low-error and under-corrects high-error subgroups---the same mechanism as global CM correction but restricted to a scalar ignoring the mixing structure between $z$-levels.
53	When $\pi_s \to 0.5$, $(1 - 2\pi_s) \to 0$ and the F-L per-subgroup correction diverges; EC-HTE's $\kappa$-guard (Section~\ref{sec:method}) avoids this singularity.
54	
55	\begin{remark}
56	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} does not require assumption~(A2).
57	For arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices ($\mathrm{FPR}_s \neq \mathrm{FNR}_s$),
58	the product form $\mathrm{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ holds exactly,
59	where $B_s = M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$, because $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$
60	follows from stochasticity of $M_s$ and $M_{\mathrm{global}}$ alone.
61	Assumption~(A2) simplifies $[B_s]_{z,1}$ to the scalar
62	$\pm \delta_s / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ but is not necessary for the product structure.
63	Under asymmetric errors, the diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) requires evaluating $[B_s]_{z,1}$ cell-by-cell rather than via a single scalar threshold; the AUC decreases from 0.86 to 0.66 (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}), reflecting the additional complexity of cell-specific error rates.
64	For binary effect modifiers ($|\mathcal{Z}|{=}2$), the asymmetric score $|[B_s]_{z,1}|$ reduces to a monotone transform of the symmetric score $|\delta_s|/((1{-}2\bar{\pi})\pi_s)$, because column-stochastic $M$ forces $|B_s[0,1]|{=}|B_s[1,1]|$; practitioners may use the simpler symmetric formula without loss.
65	See Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric} for the full derivation and empirical verification
66	($R^2 = 0.991$).
67	\end{remark}
68	
69	Assumption~(A5) simplifies exposition; the identity generalizes to subgroup-specific $\Delta\tau_s$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:a5_relaxation}, Appendix~\ref{app:a5_violation}).
70	EC-HTE's correction does not depend on (A5): each $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ corrects the local misclassification structure regardless of whether $\Delta\tau$ varies; under both positive and negative $\Delta\tau_s$--$\delta_s$ correlation, EC-HTE maintains $\geq$93\% coverage while global correction degrades to 74--82\% (Appendix~\ref{app:a5_violation}).
71	
72	The identity extends to $K > 2$ subgroups with $J$ effect-modifier levels; the multi-class bias retains the same product structure with modified amplification terms (Corollary~\ref{cor:multiclass} in Appendix~\ref{app:multiclass}).
73	
74	Assumption~(A3) ensures $M_s = C_s$; when $P(Z{=}1) \neq 0.5$, the mixing matrices acquire asymmetric entries, but the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}).
75	Empirical verification under class imbalance (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}) shows that the bias identity maintains $R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ for $K{=}2$, though EC-HTE's RMSE ratio relative to global correction increases to 1.06--1.68 as class imbalance grows.
76	In practice, NLP classification tasks often exhibit substantial class imbalance (e.g., hate speech prevalence $\ll 50\%$), and practitioners should verify that the per-subgroup expert budget threshold remains satisfied under the actual class distribution.
77	Empirical verification (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}) yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects finite-sample Monte Carlo noise, not model misspecification.
78	
79	\paragraph{Sensitivity to (A1).}
80	Assumption~(A1) is not empirically testable.
81	If misclassification correlates with potential outcomes ($\gamma = \mathrm{Corr}(\mathbb{1}[\hat{Z} {\neq} Z],\, Y(1){-}Y(0) \mid Z, S) \neq 0$), Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gains an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation; in NLP settings, this is plausible when LLM accuracy varies with outcome magnitude.
82	Sensitivity analysis frameworks~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp,cinelli2020making} can bound the degradation (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
83	
84	\paragraph{Finite-sample remainder.}
85	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is a population-level identity.
86	In practice, confusion matrices are estimated from $n_{\text{expert}}$ expert labels with $\hat{C}_s = C_s + E_s$, $\|E_s\| = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2})$; the resulting remainder is therefore $R_n = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2} \cdot \kappa(C_s))$, motivating the singularity guard ($\kappa > 100 \to$ fallback) in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
87	
88	\begin{proposition}[Debiasing Can Increase Bias]
89	\label{prop:debiasing_hurts}
90	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator ($|\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}| > |\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{naive}}|$) in subgroup $s$ if and only if
91	\begin{equation}
92	\frac{|\delta_s|}{(1 - 2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s} > 1.
93	\label{eq:hurts_condition}
94	\end{equation}
95	\end{proposition}
96	
97	Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes:
98	\begin{itemize}
99	    \item \textit{High-error} ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$): the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, excluded by~(A4); global correction always reduces bias.
100	    \item \textit{Low-error} ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$): the condition holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$---easily satisfied: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ is harmed by global correction.
101	\end{itemize}
102	The mechanism is over-correction: global inversion applies a correction calibrated for the average error rate, so low-error subgroups are overcorrected while high-error subgroups are under-corrected.
103	For subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global correction creates substantial bias---debiasing can be worse than doing nothing.
104	The bias can reverse sign across subgroups: low-error subgroups are over-corrected (bias flips from near-zero to positive) while high-error subgroups are under-corrected, a phenomenon absent from classical scalar attenuation frameworks.
105	
106	In our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}), global correction increases bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations across our parameter grid (260 of 520, excluding cases where $\Delta\pi{=}0$).
107	With the difference-in-means estimator, maximum amplification reaches $2.86\times$ for $K{=}2$ and $2.41\times$ for $K{=}4$; the mechanism operates across estimator types, with nonlinear estimators amplifying the effect further (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
108	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification across the full $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid.

%

\item[\textbf{(A1)}] \textit{Conditional independence:} misclassification depends only on the true label $Z$ and subgroup $S$, not on potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1)$.

\item[\textbf{(A4)}] \textit{Non-degeneracy:} $\pi_s \neq 0.5$ for all $s$, ensuring each $C_s$ is invertible.
\item[\textbf{(A5)}] \textit{Homogeneous treatment effects across subgroups:} $\tau(z, s) = \tau(z)$ for all $s$, so $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is a scalar.
\end{itemize}

The global mixing matrix is $M_{\text{global}} = \sum_s w_s M_s$.

\begin{theorem}[Bias Decomposition Identity]
\label{thm:bias_identity}
Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, the bias of global correction in subgroup $s$ at effect-modifier level $z$ is
\begin{align}
\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}0, s) &= +\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z0} \\
\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}1, s) &= -\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z1}
\end{align}

\end{theorem}

Equations~\eqref{eq:bias_z0}--\eqref{eq:bias_z1} constitute an exact finite-population identity, not an asymptotic approximation or bound.

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} implies that global correction trades one source of confounding for another: it removes attenuation from label noise but introduces a new bias from error-rate heterogeneity.

\paragraph{Proof sketch.}
Global correction applies $M_{\text{global}}^{-1}$ to the subgroup-specific observed CATE $\tau_{\text{obs}}(\cdot, s) = M_s \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$, yielding bias $(M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I) \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$.

\paragraph{Relationship to classical scalar attenuation.}

When $\pi_s \to 0.5$, $(1 - 2\pi_s) \to 0$ and the F-L per-subgroup correction diverges; EC-HTE's $\kappa$-guard (Section~\ref{sec:method}) avoids this singularity.

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} does not require assumption~(A2).
For arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices ($\mathrm{FPR}_s \neq \mathrm{FNR}_s$),
the product form $\mathrm{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ holds exactly,
where $B_s = M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$, because $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$
follows from stochasticity of $M_s$ and $M_{\mathrm{global}}$ alone.
Assumption~(A2) simplifies $[B_s]_{z,1}$ to the scalar
$\pm \delta_s / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ but is not necessary for the product structure.
Under asymmetric errors, the diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) requires evaluating $[B_s]_{z,1}$ cell-by-cell rather than via a single scalar threshold; the AUC decreases from 0.86 to 0.66 (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}), reflecting the additional complexity of cell-specific error rates.
For binary effect modifiers ($|\mathcal{Z}|{=}2$), the asymmetric score $|[B_s]_{z,1}|$ reduces to a monotone transform of the symmetric score $|\delta_s|/((1{-}2\bar{\pi})\pi_s)$, because column-stochastic $M$ forces $|B_s[0,1]|{=}|B_s[1,1]|$; practitioners may use the simpler symmetric formula without loss.
See Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric} for the full derivation and empirical verification
($R^2 = 0.991$).
\end{remark}

Assumption~(A5) simplifies exposition; the identity generalizes to subgroup-specific $\Delta\tau_s$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:a5_relaxation}, Appendix~\ref{app:a5_violation}).
EC-HTE's correction does not depend on (A5): each $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ corrects the local misclassification structure regardless of whether $\Delta\tau$ varies; under both positive and negative $\Delta\tau_s$--$\delta_s$ correlation, EC-HTE maintains $\geq$93\% coverage while global correction degrades to 74--82\% (Appendix~\ref{app:a5_violation}).

The identity extends to $K > 2$ subgroups with $J$ effect-modifier levels; the multi-class bias retains the same product structure with modified amplification terms (Corollary~\ref{cor:multiclass} in Appendix~\ref{app:multiclass}).

Assumption~(A3) ensures $M_s = C_s$; when $P(Z{=}1) \neq 0.5$, the mixing matrices acquire asymmetric entries, but the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}).
Empirical verification under class imbalance (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}) shows that the bias identity maintains $R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ for $K{=}2$, though EC-HTE's RMSE ratio relative to global correction increases to 1.06--1.68 as class imbalance grows.

Sensitivity analysis frameworks~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp,cinelli2020making} can bound the degradation (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\paragraph{Finite-sample remainder.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is a population-level identity.

\begin{proposition}[Debiasing Can Increase Bias]
\label{prop:debiasing_hurts}
Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator ($|\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}| > |\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{naive}}|$) in subgroup $s$ if and only if
\begin{equation}
\frac{|\delta_s|}{(1 - 2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s} > 1.
\label{eq:hurts_condition}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{High-error} ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$): the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, excluded by~(A4); global correction always reduces bias.
    \item \textit{Low-error} ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$): the condition holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$---easily satisfied: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ is harmed by global correction.
\end{itemize}
The mechanism is over-correction: global inversion applies a correction calibrated for the average error rate, so low-error subgroups are overcorrected while high-error subgroups are under-corrected.
For subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global correction creates substantial bias---debiasing can be worse than doing nothing.
The bias can reverse sign across subgroups: low-error subgroups are over-corrected (bias flips from near-zero to positive) while high-error subgroups are under-corrected, a phenomenon absent from classical scalar attenuation frameworks.

In our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}), global correction increases bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations across our parameter grid (260 of 520, excluding cases where $\Delta\pi{=}0$).
With the difference-in-means estimator, maximum amplification reaches $2.86\times$ for $K{=}2$ and $2.41\times$ for $K{=}4$; the mechanism operates across estimator types, with nonlinear estimators amplifying the effect further (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification across the full $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid.

[Director 指令] [Patch] R17 修复 — 写作批次 3（κ 分层讨论写入）

⚠️ **同样的页面约束**：主文 ≤ 8 页，每加 1 行必须压缩 1 行。

---

### 背景

MF1 要求回应 reviewer "κ≤1.25 太严、16 个 real LLM 组合无一通过" 的质疑。Agent 完成了 κ 分层分析，Reviewer 审查后给出了重要 narrative 指导。

### 关键数据发现

1. 520 synthetic configs 的 κ 全部落在 [1.43, 2.22]（DGP 结构限制，5-bin 只有 2 个 bin 有数据）
2. 合成数据 K=2：EC-HTE 在所有 κ bin 上 bias win rate ~100%，coverage ≥95%
3. **Real LLM K=4, n=250（论文主实验 budget）：EC-HTE bias win rate = 0%**
4. **但 EC-HTE coverage 始终 ≥93% vs Global 86-91%** — 这是 real LLM 场景的真正优势

### 写入要求

**主文 Section 5.4**（改写 1-2 句，不新增段落）：

将 κ≤1.25 的定位从 "applicability condition" 调整为 "sufficient condition for strongest theoretical guarantees"。参考措辞：

"A separate empirical analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}) shows that EC-HTE maintains coverage ≥93% and competitive RMSE across the κ ∈ [1.4, 3.0] range observed in real LLM confusion matrices, with the strongest bias reduction gains when n_expert ≥ 500."

**主文 Section 5.4 双阈值解释**（加 1-2 句）：

解释三层结构：
- κ>100 = Algorithm 1 数值奇异性硬保护（fallback to global）
- κ≤1.25 = 理论推荐区间（bias reduction + coverage 双优）
- κ ∈ (1.25, ~3] = 实践中 EC-HTE 仍有 **coverage 优势**（≥93% vs 86-91%），bias reduction 取决于 n_expert 和 Δπ 强度

**⚠️ 绝对不要**在主文展示 n=250 的 0% bias win rate 表格——这已在 TweetEval 段落中以自然语言承认，放表格会过度放大 negative signal。

**Appendix**（新增 ~0.5 页，不受 8 页限制）：

新建 `\subsection{κ Stratification Analysis}` (label: app:kappa_analysis)，放两个表：
(a) 合成数据 κ 分层：κ bin、n_configs、mean bias reduction、RMSE ratio、win rate、coverage — 展示 EC-HTE 无偏性（强项）
(b) Real LLM κ 分层 × n_expert 交叉表：展示 coverage 在所有组合下 ≥93%

合成数据表的 κ bins 用实际数据分布（2-bin：κ≤1.8 vs κ>1.8，或按 median split），不要用原来的 5-bin（3 个空 bin 看起来不好）。

**Limitations**（检查/微调）：

确认现有 κ≤1.25 相关讨论与新写入的 Section 5.4 一致。如有矛盾，统一为 "sufficient condition" 叙事。

---

### Narrative 核心逻辑

Reviewer 可能的 challenge：κ≤1.25 没有 LLM 通过 → 方法不实用。

我们的 defense：
1. κ≤1.25 是 sufficient condition，非 necessary — 方法在更宽 κ 范围仍有效
2. EC-HTE 在 real LLM 场景的核心价值是 **calibrated inference**（coverage ≥93%），不只是 bias reduction
3. Bias reduction 在足够 n_expert (≥500) 下也实现 — 这是 expert budget 与 correction quality 的合理 tradeoff

这个叙事必须自然融入现有段落，不要给人"在 defend 一个弱点"的感觉——而是"characterizing the operating regime"。

This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}
